Title: Hybrid Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Social Network Community Detection Framework for Optimal Management and Redesign of Urban Water Network
Author: Sajjad Ali Ettyem; Hasan Ziafat; Jafaar Fahad A. Rida; Sanaz Asadini
Full study title: Hybrid Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Social Network Community Detection Framework for Optimal Management and Redesign of Urban Water Network.
Journal or conference: Journal of Resource Management and Decision Engineering.
Study funding sources: The authors explicitly state that the study received no financial support.
Possible conflicts of interest for study: None declared. The authors explicitly report no conflict of interest.
Network type: Real-world urban water distribution network (Thi-Qar, Iraq), evaluated through computational modelling and optimisation. The study uses a real-world network case study but reports computational rather than field-deployment evaluation.
Sensor type and sensing modality:
Water-quality monitoring sensors for detecting contamination events in the water distribution network. The sensor-placement formulation considers candidate junction locations and evaluates contamination detection time, contaminated-water volume and detection likelihood.

The paper separately reports 10 flow meters installed in the network. These flow meters should not be confused with the water-quality sensors being optimised.
Study location: Thi-Qar, Iraq, in the southwest of the country. The network is supplied by the Euphrates River and the Al-Gharraf stream.
Number of nodes/junctions: Not reported. The article does not explicitly provide the total number of network junctions.
Number of pipes: Not reported. The article does not explicitly provide the total number of pipes.
Number of sensors considered:
The water-quality sensor-placement formulation uses a fixed sensor-budget parameter \(M\):
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=M
\]
However, the numerical value of \(M\) is not reported in the article.

The authors separately report 10 installed flow meters (\(N_{fm}=10\)). These are flow-monitoring devices and should not be interpreted as the number of water-quality sensors selected by the optimisation.
Number of pumps and valves: Not reported as numerical counts. The paper discusses pump operations and valve/boundary interventions but does not provide complete counts of pumps and valves.
Network size classification: Not reported. The authors describe the Thi-Qar network as an urban water distribution network but do not explicitly classify it as small, medium or large.
Aim of study:
The study aims to develop and evaluate a hybrid reinforcement-learning and social-network community-detection framework integrating Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Social Network Search (SNS), edge-betweenness-based community partitioning and multi-objective optimisation. The framework is designed for the optimal sectorisation, monitoring and redesign of the Thi-Qar urban water distribution network while simultaneously improving water-quality detection, hydraulic performance and topological efficiency.

The water-quality component specifically addresses minimising expected contamination detection time, minimising expected contaminated-water volume and maximising contamination detection likelihood.
Simulation and experimental environment:
The study evaluates the proposed framework using the Thi-Qar urban water distribution network in Iraq. The network is represented as a graph in which junctions correspond to nodes and pipes correspond to edges. The case-study network serves approximately 650,000 inhabitants and is supplied by the Euphrates River and the Al-Gharraf stream.

The network is organised into seven District Metered Areas (DMAs), with four broader optimised zones identified in the reported analysis. The model uses a uniform design pressure of 20 m at each node and reports 10 installed flow meters. The analysis considers the main flow pipes.

The water-quality sensor-placement subproblem is formulated as a multi-objective optimisation problem using three criteria: expected contamination detection time, expected contaminated-water volume and detection likelihood. Candidate sensor locations are represented by a binary decision vector over network junctions, subject to a fixed sensor-budget constraint.

The framework integrates PPO-based reinforcement learning, NSGA-II, roulette-wheel selection, Social Network Search and edge-betweenness-based community detection. The PPO agent adaptively guides optimisation by tuning objective weights and refining candidate solutions. Hydraulic, topological and water-quality performance are subsequently evaluated.

The article does not clearly identify the hydraulic simulation software, software version, programming language, deep-learning library or computational hardware used.
Notes:
This study combines water-network sectorisation, community detection, hydraulic optimisation and water-quality sensor placement within a single framework.

An important distinction is that the water-quality sensor-placement subproblem is formulated over candidate junctions, whereas the wider social-network and community-detection framework operates on network nodes and edges.

The 10 flow meters reported by the authors are not equivalent to the water-quality sensor budget. The numerical water-quality sensor budget \(M\) is not specified.

The study uses PPO as its reinforcement-learning component, NSGA-II for multi-objective sensor-configuration evolution, and Social Network Search for population-based search and community-related optimisation. These methods have distinct roles and should not be treated as interchangeable algorithms.
Main methodological contributions:
The study proposes a hybrid reinforcement-learning and social-network community-detection framework for water distribution network sectorisation, monitoring and redesign. Its methodology integrates Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II), Social Network Search (SNS), edge-betweenness-based community detection and multi-objective optimisation.

For the water-quality monitoring component, sensor placement is formulated as a multi-objective optimisation problem using a binary decision vector representing sensor presence or absence at candidate network junctions. The framework considers three objectives: minimising expected contamination detection time, minimising expected contaminated-water volume and maximising contamination detection likelihood.

The sensor-placement procedure uses demand-weighted roulette-wheel selection to generate an initial subdomain of candidate junctions. NSGA-II evolves candidate sensor configurations to produce a Pareto front, while non-dominated solutions are retained across successive generations. PPO provides an adaptive reinforcement-learning component that guides optimisation through reward-based policy updates and adjustment of objective weights.

The wider framework combines SNS search behaviours—imitation, conversation, disputation and innovation—with edge-betweenness-based community detection to support network partitioning and sectorisation.
Overall study findings:
The authors report that the proposed RL-enhanced framework improves several hydraulic and topological performance indicators in the Thi-Qar network.

The resilience deviation index decreases from 8.69 to 2.60, representing an approximately 70% reduction. The balance index improves from 1.27 to 1.01, while modularity increases from 0.72 to 0.79, an improvement of approximately 9.7%.

Average path length decreases from 9.82 to 8.65, representing an approximately 11.9% reduction, while average path-length deviation decreases from 12.36 to 6.98, a reduction of approximately 43.5%. The standard deviation of nodal pressure decreases from 5.72 to 5.12, indicating improved pressure uniformity.

For water-quality monitoring, the authors report that the proposed framework simultaneously addresses minimising expected detection time, minimising contaminated-water volume and maximising detection likelihood.

The reported results demonstrate the potential of combining reinforcement learning, evolutionary optimisation and social-network methods for integrated water-network sectorisation and monitoring. However, the paper does not provide a clear numerical comparison of the sensor-placement component against standalone sensor-placement algorithms.
Research gaps and future directions:
The authors identify the need to validate the proposed framework across water distribution networks with different sizes, layouts, source configurations and levels of hydraulic complexity, including megacity-scale systems and networks with intermittent supply.

They recommend introducing uncertainty in water demand, pipe roughness, contamination occurrence, equipment availability and future network expansion. They also identify dynamic DMA management, more detailed water-quality processes and economic objectives as areas requiring further investigation.

The authors further suggest comparing deterministic and stochastic optimisation formulations and evaluating alternative reinforcement-learning algorithms, evolutionary methods, graph neural networks and conventional multi-objective metaheuristics.

They identify field implementation and digital-twin integration as important next steps for evaluating the framework under real operational constraints.

From the perspective of this review, additional opportunities include reporting the numerical water-quality sensor budget, evaluating sensor deployment costs, providing reproducible sensor-placement configurations and isolating the contribution of PPO to the sensor-placement component. These are reviewer observations rather than explicit author-stated recommendations.
Study limitations:
The authors acknowledge that the framework was evaluated on a single case-study network in Thi-Qar. Network-specific characteristics, including topology, demand distribution, source configuration and existing infrastructure, may influence algorithm performance and limit generalisability.

Only selected hydraulic, topological and water-quality criteria are included. Other potentially important factors, such as lifecycle costs, pipe failure probabilities, valve reliability, energy tariffs, chlorine decay, stochastic contamination behaviour and emergency firefighting demand, are not explicitly modelled.

The analysis is based on modelled network conditions rather than continuous real-time operation. Consequently, sensor failure, telemetry delays, uncertain demand, inaccurate hydraulic parameters and incomplete field data are not examined.

The authors also acknowledge that computational requirements, hyperparameter sensitivity, convergence behaviour and robustness across alternative initialisations require more systematic investigation.
Reproducibility and data availability:
The study evaluates the Thi-Qar urban water distribution network and provides methodological descriptions of the PPO, NSGA-II, SNS and community-detection components. It also reports the mathematical formulation of the three water-quality sensor-placement objectives, the fixed sensor-budget constraint and several hydraulic and topological performance results.

The authors state that data are available for research purposes upon reasonable request to the corresponding author. However, the article does not identify a public repository containing the complete source code, trained models, configuration files or processed experimental results.

The programming language, hydraulic simulation software, software versions, hardware specifications and numerical water-quality sensor budget are not sufficiently documented in the article. These omissions limit independent reproduction of the complete framework.
RL algorithm:
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO).

PPO is the core reinforcement-learning algorithm used to guide the optimisation process. The agent interacts iteratively with the environment and updates its policy using reward feedback. The authors describe PPO as an adaptive decision-making mechanism that guides the optimisation by tuning objective weights and refining candidate solutions.
RL architecture:
The framework uses an Actor-Critic architecture. The Actor represents the policy \(\pi(s_t)\), which defines the probability distribution over possible actions, while the Critic estimates the state-value function \(V(s_t)\).

The PPO agent uses Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) to estimate the advantage of actions from temporal-difference information. Policy updates employ the PPO clipping mechanism to limit excessively large policy changes and support stable learning.

The article also describes the integration of the RL agent within a behaviour-tree decision-making structure. However, the exact neural-network layer configuration, number of neurons, activation functions and software implementation are not reported.
Sensor placement approach:
The water-quality sensor-placement problem is formulated as a multi-objective optimisation problem over candidate network junctions.

A binary decision vector represents the presence or absence of a sensor at each candidate junction:
\[
X=[x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n]
\]
Demand-weighted roulette-wheel selection is used to generate an initial subdomain of candidate junctions. NSGA-II then evolves candidate sensor configurations to identify a Pareto-optimal front.

Non-dominated configurations are retained in subsequent generations, while roulette-wheel selection fills the remaining candidate positions. This iterative process refines the solution space and evaluates candidate sensor configurations against contamination detection time, contaminated-water volume and detection likelihood.

PPO adaptively guides the broader optimisation process by adjusting objective weights and refining candidate solutions. SNS and edge-betweenness-based community detection support the wider network-sectorisation framework.
The article does not establish that PPO independently selects individual sensor locations. Instead, PPO guides the broader optimisation process, while roulette-wheel selection and NSGA-II perform the explicitly described candidate-generation and sensor-configuration search operations.
State representation:
For the general PPO framework, the article defines the state as a combination of agent positional information, relevant task features and a representation of the environmental map.
The article defines the PPO state as a combination of:
- Agent positional information.
- Relevant task features.
- A representation of the environmental map.
The MDP transition is represented by:
\[
(s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1})
\]
The sensor-placement decision itself is represented by a binary vector:
\[
X=[x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n]
\]
where \(x_i\) indicates whether a sensor is present at candidate junction \(i\).

The article does not provide a complete, explicit numerical state vector for the water-quality sensor-placement subproblem. The general MDP state description and the sensor-placement decision vector should therefore be distinguished.
Action space:
The PPO agent selects actions within the MDP framework to guide the optimisation process. The article describes the action as a decision intended to maximise the action-value function and improve the expected cumulative reward.

For sensor placement, the candidate configuration is represented by the binary decision vector \(X\), in which each element indicates whether a sensor is placed at a candidate junction.

However, the article does not explicitly provide a complete action-space definition specifying the exact PPO action corresponding to each individual sensor-placement decision. It is therefore safer not to claim that PPO directly selects each sensor location sequentially.
Reward function:
The article defines the PPO reward as a weighted function incorporating task importance, completion effectiveness and collaborative efficiency among agents.

However, it does not provide a complete explicit mathematical reward equation specifically for the water-quality sensor-placement subproblem.

The three sensor-placement objectives are separately defined as:
1. Minimise expected contamination detection time.
2. Minimise expected contaminated-water volume.
3. Maximise contamination detection likelihood.
These objective functions should not be presented as a fully specified PPO reward equation because the article does not explicitly establish that equivalence.
Comparator algorithms:
The article compares the proposed RL-enhanced framework with a non-RL configuration for the broader water-network sectorisation and performance assessment.

The non-RL configuration provides the baseline for comparing hydraulic and topological indicators.

NSGA-II and SNS are components of the proposed hybrid framework, not independent comparator algorithms in the reported RL-versus-non-RL comparison.

The article does not provide a comprehensive sensor-placement comparison against standalone GA, PSO or other conventional sensor-placement algorithms.
Hyperparameter optimisation:
Not reported as a separate systematic hyperparameter-optimisation procedure.

The article describes PPO policy updates and the use of a clipping parameter, but it does not provide a grid search, Bayesian optimisation or other explicit systematic hyperparameter-tuning procedure.
RL training strategy:
The PPO agent is trained through iterative interaction with the environment using an Actor-Critic learning architecture.

At each interaction, the agent observes the current state, selects an action according to its policy and receives a reward based on task importance, completion effectiveness and collaborative efficiency. The environment then transitions to a new state.

The Critic estimates the state-value function \(V(s_t)\), while Generalized Advantage Estimation is used to calculate action advantages. PPO updates the policy using its clipped objective to prevent excessively large policy changes.

Within the wider optimisation framework, demand-weighted roulette-wheel selection generates candidate junction subdomains, and NSGA-II evolves sensor-placement configurations. Non-dominated solutions are retained across generations, while the remaining candidate positions are filled through roulette-wheel selection.

The SNS component introduces imitation, conversation, disputation and innovation search behaviours to balance exploitation and exploration.

The authors do not report a numerical PPO training-episode count, learning rate, discount factor, batch size, replay-buffer capacity, target-network update interval or explicit convergence threshold.
Constraints on sensor placement:
The water-quality sensor-placement formulation imposes a fixed sensor-budget constraint:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=M
\]
where:
- \(x_i\) indicates whether a sensor is installed at candidate junction \(i\).
- \(n\) is the number of candidate junctions.
- \(M\) is the specified number of sensors.
The sensor-placement decision is therefore restricted to exactly \(M\) selected locations.

The article does not report the numerical value of \(M\). It also does not provide explicit numerical sensor-spacing, installation-cost or location-accessibility constraints.
Detection coverage:
The article evaluates detection likelihood rather than reporting a conventional percentage detection-coverage metric.

Detection likelihood is defined as:
\[
f_3=\frac{1}{N_s}\sum_{s=1}^{N_s}d_s(X)
\]
where \(d_s=1\) if contamination event \(s\) is detected and \(0\) otherwise.

The authors report this measure as the proportion of contamination events detected by the selected sensor configuration. A complete network-wide percentage coverage value is not explicitly provided in the extracted numerical results.
Detection accuracy: Not reported as conventional classification accuracy. The study evaluates contamination detection likelihood, rather than precision, recall, F1-score or false-positive rate.
Detection time:
Expected contamination detection time is a principal optimisation objective.

For each contamination event, the detection time is defined as the earliest detection time among the selected sensor locations:
\[
t_d^s(X)=\min_{x_i=1}\{t_d(x_i)\}
\]
The overall objective is to minimise the average detection time across contamination events.

The article provides normalised detection-time values for selected zones, including a reported value of 0.85 for Zone 4. It does not provide a complete numerical table of absolute detection times in seconds or minutes for the entire network.
Sensor deployment cost: Not reported as a numerical sensor deployment cost. The article discusses the practical need to allocate monitoring resources selectively but does not quantify sensor purchase, installation or maintenance costs
Number of sensors selected:
The numerical sensor budget \(M\) is not reported. The paper specifies the fixed-budget constraint but does not state the number of water-quality sensors selected.

The 10 flow meters reported in the network description are not the final water-quality sensor count.
Computational performance:
The study reports improvements in hydraulic and topological performance, including pressure uniformity, resilience deviation, balance, modularity and average path length.

However, it does not provide a detailed numerical evaluation of PPO training time, total optimisation runtime, memory requirements or computational complexity.

The authors acknowledge that computational requirements, convergence behaviour, hyperparameter sensitivity and robustness across alternative initialisations require further investigation.
Comparative performance:
The proposed RL-enhanced framework is compared with a non-RL configuration for hydraulic and topological performance.

The principal reported improvements include:
- Resilience deviation index: 8.69 to 2.60, approximately 70% reduction.
- Balance index: 1.27 to 1.01.
- Modularity: 0.72 to 0.79, approximately 9.7% improvement.
- Average path length: 9.82 to 8.65, approximately 11.9% reduction.
- Average path-length deviation: 12.36 to 6.98, approximately 43.5% reduction.
- Standard deviation of nodal pressure: 5.72 to 5.12, approximately 10.5% reduction.
For water-quality monitoring, the authors report that the proposed framework addresses all three objectives simultaneously. However, the paper does not provide a sufficiently detailed standalone sensor-placement comparison to attribute all the reported hydraulic and topological improvements specifically to the sensor-placement component.
Main quantitative results:
The authors report improvements in several hydraulic and topological indicators under the RL-enhanced configuration compared with the configuration without RL. The resilience deviation index decreased from 8.69 to 2.60, the balance index from 1.27 to 1.01, and the standard deviation of nodal pressure from 5.72 to 5.12. The modularity index increased from 0.72 to 0.79, while average path length decreased from 9.82 to 8.65 and average path-length deviation from 12.36 to 6.98. Other reported indicators included minimum, mean and maximum nodal pressure, resilience index, and total and worst edge cuts.

The seven DMA sizes under the RL-enhanced configuration were 46, 46, 46, 46, 47, 46 and 49 nodes, compared with a range of 38–54 nodes without RL.

For water-quality monitoring, the authors reported normalised values of 0.85 for expected detection time in Zone 4, 0.65 for contaminated-water volume in Zone 2, and 0.79 for detection likelihood in Zone 4. These are normalised values and should not be interpreted as absolute time, volume or percentage measurements.
Evaluation metrics and measurement crite:
The water-quality sensor-placement component uses three primary metrics:
1. Expected detection time: Average earliest detection time across the simulated contamination events.
2. Expected contaminated-water volume: Average volume of contaminated water across network junctions and time steps until detection.
3. Detection likelihood: Proportion of contamination events detected by the selected sensor configuration.
The wider sectorisation framework also evaluates:
- Minimum nodal pressure.
- Mean nodal pressure.
- Maximum nodal pressure.
- Standard deviation of nodal pressure.
- Resilience index.
- Resilience deviation index.
- Balance index.
- Total and worst number of edge cuts.
- Modularity index.
- Average path length.
- Average path-length deviation.
- Adjusted Mutual Information (AMI) for community-partition similarity.
The paper distinguishes water-quality objectives from hydraulic and topological performance indicators. These should remain separate in the extraction and subsequent synthesis.
Hydraulic simulation software: Not reported. The article discusses hydraulic and water-quality modelling but does not identify a specific simulation package or software version.
RL framework or library: Not reported. PPO and the Actor-Critic architecture are described, but no specific software library such as PyTorch or TensorFlow is identified.
Dataset or benchmark source:
Thi-Qar urban water distribution network, Iraq. The network is described as being supplied by the Euphrates River and the Al-Gharraf stream.

The article does not provide a public repository or DOI for the network input files.
Experimental scenarios:
The study evaluates the hybrid framework on the Thi-Qar urban water distribution network.

The experiments investigate:
- Water-network sectorisation into seven DMAs.

- Water-quality sensor placement for contamination detection.
- Minimisation of expected contamination detection time.

Training episodes: Not reported. The article describes iterative PPO policy learning but does not provide a numerical episode count.

Title: Domain Knowledge-Based Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning for Sensor Placement
Author: Mingxuan Song; Chengyu Hu; Wenyin Gong; Xuesong Yan
Full study title: Domain Knowledge-Based Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning for Sensor Placement
Possible conflicts of interest for study: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
Network type: Simulated water supply network (WSN), represented as a network of nodes and pipes and modelled for contamination-event detection.
Sensor type and sensing modality: Water-quality sensors for monitoring and detecting pollutant/contamination events. The sensor-placement algorithm selects network nodes at which these sensors are to be installed.
Study location: Not reported (the geographical location of the experimental network is not specified).
Number of sensors considered: The numerical sensor budget and final number of sensors selected in the 126-node experimental network are not explicitly reported. Figure 1 presents an illustrative nine-node network with two sensors, but this example does not establish the sensor count used in the main experiment.
Number of reservoirs and tanks: 1 source and 2 tanks, as reported by the authors.
Network size classification: 126 nodes; the authors do not explicitly classify the network as small, medium, or large.
Aim of study: The study aims to formulate the sensor placement problem in water supply networks as a sequential decision optimisation problem and develop a domain knowledge-based Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (ERL) algorithm to identify effective sensor combinations. The proposed approach incorporates prior domain knowledge into the reinforcement learning model to improve the selection of sensor locations and reduce pollutant detection time.
Simulation and experimental environment: The study evaluates sensor placement for contamination-event detection in a simulated water supply network modelled as a network of nodes and pipes. The experimental network contains 126 nodes, 168 pipes, one source, two tanks, two pumps and eight valves. EPANET is used for hydraulic and water-quality simulation, with a five-minute simulation time step over a 96-hour period. The network's EPANET input files are obtained from the Exeter Centre for Water Systems (ECWS). The proposed domain knowledge-based Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (ERL) algorithm is evaluated against Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) approaches. The specific EPANET version, programming language, reinforcement learning library and computational hardware are not reported.
Notes: In this article, WSN refers to water supply network, not wireless sensor network. Figure 1 presents an illustrative small network with nine nodes, two sources, one tank and 13 pipes; these are not the characteristics of the experimental network. The experimental network is separately described as having 126 nodes and 168 pipes. The authors do not identify a specific benchmark network name or geographical study location. The numerical sensor budget and final number of sensors selected in the 126-node experiment are not explicitly reported; the two sensors shown in Figure 1 belong only to the illustrative nine-node example.
Main methodological contributions: The study proposes a domain knowledge-based Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (ERL) algorithm for sensor placement in water supply networks. The authors formulate sensor placement as a sequential decision optimisation problem and develop a population-based learning approach that combines policy-gradient-based reinforcement learning with evolutionary computation. The proposed method incorporates prior domain knowledge derived from the individual pollutant detection-time performance of candidate sensor locations into the learning process. A pointer-network architecture is used to select sensor locations sequentially, while evolutionary operations, including crossover and mutation, are applied to improve the population of learning agents. The proposed approach is evaluated against Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) methods, with the objective of reducing pollutant detection time.
Overall study findings: The experimental results indicate that the proposed domain knowledge-based Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (ERL) algorithm achieved better sensor-placement performance than the meta-heuristic algorithms and deep reinforcement learning (DRL) comparator. The authors report that modelling sensor placement as a sequential decision optimisation problem improved the search process compared with conventional optimisation approaches. Incorporating prior domain knowledge, based on the individual detection-time performance of candidate sensor locations, further improved the ERL algorithm's search performance. Overall, the study demonstrates the potential of combining reinforcement learning, evolutionary computation and domain knowledge to identify sensor combinations that reduce pollutant detection time in water supply networks.
Research gaps and future directions:
The authors identify the difficulty of solving sensor placement problems in large-scale water supply networks because the decision space increases rapidly with network size. They also discuss challenges associated with conventional deep reinforcement learning, including sparse-reward credit assignment, inadequate exploration and sensitivity to hyperparameters. The article highlights a trade-off between incorporating domain knowledge to improve algorithm performance and maintaining the generalisation ability of the model. Although the proposed ERL approach demonstrates improved performance, the authors describe the work as an initial demonstration of the feasibility and efficiency of applying ERL to sensor placement.

The article does not explicitly provide a detailed future-work agenda. From the perspective of this review, further research opportunities include testing ERL on additional benchmark and real-world water distribution networks, evaluating its generalisation under different contamination scenarios and network uncertainties, and investigating scalability to larger networks. Further comparative evaluation, reproducibility through publicly available implementations and datasets, and assessment of the transferability of domain knowledge across networks would also strengthen the evidence base. These additional opportunities are review observations rather than explicit recommendations attributed to the authors.
Study limitations:
The authors do not provide a separately structured or comprehensive statement of study limitations. However, the study identifies challenges associated with sensor placement in large-scale water supply networks, particularly the exponential growth of the decision space and computational complexity as network size increases. The proposed approach also relies on prior domain knowledge obtained by measuring individual sensor detection times across a set of pollution events. This introduces a requirement for preliminary evaluation of candidate sensor locations before the knowledge can be incorporated into the ERL model. The authors further report that Monte Carlo-based initial sequence generation was not particularly effective and that using independent population individuals without information sharing produced only a slight improvement in detection time.

From a critical review perspective, the evidence presented does not establish the generalisability of the proposed method across a broad range of independently validated real-world networks. The article also does not provide sufficient evidence in the material reviewed to assess operational deployment, transferability of learned policies or performance under changing network conditions. These are reviewer-identified evidence limitations, not limitations explicitly acknowledged by the authors.
Reproducibility and data availability: The study uses the open-source EPANET software to simulate the hydraulic and water-quality behaviour of the water supply network and the effects of contamination events. The authors state that the EPANET input files for the network can be obtained from the Exeter Centre for Water Systems (ECWS). The article therefore identifies publicly accessible sources for the simulation software and network input files. However, the Data Availability Statement does not explicitly provide a repository or download link for the authors’ ERL implementation, source code, trained models, or processed experimental results. The article reports important experimental configuration details, including the network characteristics, simulation time step and duration, and selected algorithm hyperparameters, which provide some methodological information for replication. Nevertheless, the availability of the original implementation and complete experimental data cannot be confirmed from the article.
RL algorithm: Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (ERL), specifically a domain knowledge-based Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning algorithm. The method combines policy-gradient-based deep reinforcement learning with an evolutionary strategy. Each population individual contains a neural-network-based agent that learns a stochastic policy for sequential sensor-node selection. The population evolves through genetic-algorithm-inspired crossover and mutation operations. Domain knowledge, derived from individual sensor-node detection times across pollution events, is incorporated into the neural-network input to improve the search process.
RL architecture: The proposed ERL uses a population-based architecture in which each individual is an agent represented by a neural network-based pointer network. The pointer network consists of one 128-unit fully connected feedforward linear layer, followed by an encoder and a decoder, each implemented using recurrent neural network (RNN) modules with 128 long short-term memory (LSTM) units. The encoder transforms the input features into a sequence of latent representations, while the decoder uses an attention-based pointing mechanism to select sensor nodes sequentially. The attention mechanism uses two parameter matrices and an attention vector to calculate selection probabilities. A masking mechanism prevents previously selected nodes from being selected again. Each agent learns a stochastic policy using policy-gradient optimisation and stochastic gradient descent. At the population level, neural-network parameters are encoded as chromosomes and evolved through crossover and mutation operations. Domain knowledge, derived from individual sensor detection-time measurements, is incorporated into the neural-network input.
Sensor placement approach: The study formulates water-quality sensor placement as a sequential decision optimisation problem using a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Sensor locations are selected one at a time from the available network nodes. The initial state is an N-dimensional binary vector, where each element indicates whether a sensor has been placed at a candidate node. At each decision step, the ERL agent selects one previously unselected node, updates the state and continues until the required number of sensors has been placed. A pointer network generates a probability distribution over candidate nodes, while a masking mechanism prevents the repeated selection of previously chosen locations. The algorithm uses probabilistic node selection and parallel exploration of multiple candidate solutions to improve the search process. At the inference stage, multiple feasible sensor combinations are generated, and the combination with the shortest detection time is selected. The evolutionary component improves the policy through population-level crossover and mutation, while domain knowledge derived from individual sensor detection-time measurements guides the selection process.
State representation:
The state is represented by an N-dimensional binary vector:

\(x = [x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N]\)

where \(N\) is the total number of candidate nodes at which sensors can be installed. Each element \(x_i\) takes a binary value: 0 indicates that no sensor has been placed at node \(i\), while 1 indicates that a sensor has been placed there. The initial state is an all-zero vector. Each sensor-placement action changes the selected node's value from 0 to 1, while previously selected nodes retain their values. The process continues until the required number of sensors has been placed. The final binary vector therefore identifies the selected sensor locations. The state representation also accounts for previously selected nodes when determining subsequent placement actions.
Action space:
The action space consists of selecting one candidate network node at each decision step. An action is represented by an N-dimensional binary vector:

\(a = [a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_N]\)

where \(a_i \in \{0,1\}\), and exactly one element is equal to 1. A value of 1 indicates the node selected for sensor placement in the current step, while all other elements are 0. The selected node must not have been chosen previously. A masking mechanism in the pointer network prevents the selection of previously selected nodes. Each action adds one sensor to the current configuration, and the process continues until the required number of sensors has been selected.
Reward function:
The ERL algorithm uses the expected minimum pollutant detection time as its optimisation objective. For a selected sensor combination, the detection time for each pollution event is the earliest time at which any selected sensor detects a non-zero pollutant concentration. The average minimum detection time across the pollution-event set is calculated and used to evaluate the selected sensor combination.

The policy is updated using a policy-gradient method. The gradient incorporates the difference between the detection time \(t_j\) of the current candidate solution and an exponential moving average baseline \(b\):
\[
(t_j-b)\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(S|V)
\]
The baseline is updated using:
\[
b'_j=\alpha b_j+(1-\alpha)t_j
\]
where \(\alpha\) is the baseline smoothing coefficient. The algorithm seeks to minimise detection time: solutions with shorter detection times relative to the baseline influence the policy update favourably. The authors use stochastic gradient descent to update the neural-network parameters.
Optimisation objectives: The primary objective is to minimise the average pollutant detection time across the considered pollution events by identifying an effective combination of water-quality sensor locations. For each pollution event, the detection time is determined by the earliest time at which at least one selected sensor detects a non-zero pollutant concentration. The ERL algorithm therefore seeks a sensor configuration that reduces the average minimum detection time across the event set. The study also considers the computational efficiency of the search process and the ability of the proposed method to identify effective sensor combinations in large-scale water supply networks.
Comparator algorithms:
The proposed domain knowledge-based ERL algorithm is evaluated against two principal comparator algorithms:
1. Genetic Algorithm (GA): A population-based evolutionary optimisation algorithm in which each chromosome represents a sensor-placement configuration. The GA uses parent selection, multiple-point crossover and single-point mutation to generate successive populations.
2. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL): A neural-network-based reinforcement learning approach that uses the same underlying network architecture as the ERL agents but does not incorporate the evolutionary population mechanisms.
The study also conducts internal ERL ablation and configuration comparisons, examining the effects of domain knowledge, probabilistic versus greedy node selection, multi-threaded search and evolutionary computation operators. These are component-level comparisons within ERL rather than separate baseline algorithms.
Hyperparameter optimisation: The study does not report the use of an automated hyperparameter optimisation method such as grid search or Bayesian optimisation. Instead, the authors specify algorithm hyperparameters and conduct sensitivity experiments to examine the effects of different ERL components and configurations. For the DRL comparator, the mini-batch size is 512, the search step length is 500, the learning rate is \(1 \times 10^{-2}\), the baseline attenuation coefficient is \(\alpha = 0.99\), and the gradient norm is clipped to 1.0. Neural-network parameters are initially sampled uniformly from the interval \((-0.8, 0.8)\). For ERL, the crossover and mutation probabilities are both set to 0.6 and 0.1, respectively. The GA comparator also uses crossover and mutation probabilities of 0.6 and 0.1, respectively, and terminates after 500 generations. The ERL sensitivity experiments investigate the effects of domain knowledge, initial sequence generation, population evolution and node-selection strategies.
RL training strategy:
The proposed Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (ERL) algorithm uses an iterative, population-based training strategy that combines policy-gradient learning with evolutionary computation. Initially, a population of neural-network-based agents is created, with each individual representing an ERL policy. Each agent generates candidate sensor combinations through sequential node selection using its stochastic policy. The detection time of each candidate combination is evaluated against the pollution-event set, and the policy parameters are updated using policy-gradient optimisation and stochastic gradient descent. An exponential moving average baseline is incorporated into the gradient update.

Following the individual learning stage, the population undergoes evolutionary operations. Neural-network parameters are encoded as chromosomes and modified through crossover and mutation. The crossover and mutation probabilities are set to 0.6 and 0.1, respectively. Individual policy learning and population evolution are repeated iteratively until the stopping condition is reached. The authors report the algorithm comparison after 500 iterations.

The training strategy also incorporates parallel exploration and probabilistic node selection. Multiple candidate sensor combinations are explored, and the best-performing combination, based on pollutant detection time, is retained. Domain knowledge derived from individual sensor detection-time measurements is supplied as prior input to guide policy learning.
Constraints on sensor placement:
The sensor-placement problem is subject to a fixed sensor-budget constraint: only a limited, predetermined number of sensors can be installed across the candidate network nodes. The placement process must continue until the specified number of sensors has been selected. Each sensor must occupy a distinct candidate node; therefore, duplicate placement at the same node is prohibited. The action-selection mechanism enforces this restriction through a masking array that prevents previously selected nodes from being selected again.

The study also recognises practical deployment constraints, including the economic costs of purchasing, installing and maintaining water-quality sensors, as well as geographical and network-layout limitations. However, these practical considerations are discussed as motivations for limiting sensor deployment rather than being implemented as separate cost or geographical constraints in the ERL optimisation formulation.
Detection coverage: The study does not explicitly report detection coverage as a percentage or as the proportion of pollution events detected by the selected sensor configuration. Instead, it evaluates sensor-placement performance using the average minimum detection time across a set of pollution events. A pollution event is considered detected when at least one selected sensor first registers a non-zero pollutant concentration. If none of the selected sensors detects an event during the simulation period, the detection time for that event is assigned the full simulation duration (96 hours). Therefore, detection coverage as a separate quantitative metric is not reported.
Detection accuracy: The study does not report detection accuracy as a percentage, nor does it calculate conventional classification metrics such as precision, recall, F1-score or false-positive rate. Instead, sensor-placement performance is evaluated by measuring the average minimum pollutant detection time across a set of pollution events. A pollution event is detected when at least one selected sensor first registers a non-zero pollutant concentration. Events not detected within the simulation period are assigned the full simulation duration as their detection time. Consequently, the study evaluates the timeliness of contamination detection rather than detection accuracy as a separate quantitative metric.
Detection time:
Detection time is the principal performance metric used to evaluate the proposed ERL sensor-placement approach. For each pollution event, it is measured as the elapsed time between the occurrence of contamination and the first detection of a non-zero pollutant concentration by any selected sensor. The study calculates the minimum detection time for each event and then determines the average minimum detection time across the pollution-event set. If an event is not detected during the simulation period, its detection time is assigned the full simulation duration of 96 hours.

However, the article does not provide a comprehensive numerical comparison of total execution time, CPU time, memory consumption or hardware utilisation. Title: SPARC: Sensor Placement for Accurate Risk Contaminant Detection in Water Distribution Networks Using Deep Q-Network and Grid Search
Author: Fadelis Sukya; Ary Mazharuddin Shiddiqi; Saad Ali Alahmari; Ervin Nurhayati; Anton Satria Prabuwono; Arif Bramantoro; Fawaz Delaim Alharbi
Full study title: SPARC: Sensor Placement for Accurate Risk Contaminant Detection in Water Distribution Networks Using Deep Q-Network and Grid Search.
Study funding sources: The study was supported and funded by the Deanship of Scientific Research at Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University (IMSIU), grant number IMSIU-DDRSP2602.
Network or benchmark name:
The study uses four water distribution network benchmark datasets:
- FOS (Fossiron)
- JILIN
- ZJ
- BWSN
Network type: Simulated benchmark water distribution networks. The networks are represented using graph-based structures consisting of nodes and links, with hydraulic and contamination propagation behaviour simulated using EPANET.
Sensor type and sensing modality: Water-quality sensors for detecting contaminant events in clean water distribution networks. The sensors are positioned at selected network nodes to monitor contamination propagation and identify contamination scenarios.
Study location: Not applicable (benchmark networks). The experiments use benchmark network datasets rather than a geographically identified real-world WDN case study.
Number of nodes/junctions: FOS: 36 junctions; JILIN: 27 junctions; BWSN: 128 junctions; ZJ: 114 junctions.
Number of pipes: FOS: 58 pipes; JILIN: 34 pipes; BWSN: 169 pipes; ZJ: 184 pipes.
Number of sensors considered: A fixed budget of K = 10 sensors is used across all four benchmark networks. Each DQN episode involves selecting 10 sensor locations, with a maximum of 10 placement steps per episode.
Number of reservoirs and tanks:
Number of reservoirs and tanks:
- FOS: 1 reservoir and 0 tanks.
- JILIN: 1 reservoir and 3 tanks.
- ZJ: 2 reservoirs and 2 tanks.
- BWSN: 1 reservoir and 2 tanks.
Number of pumps and valves: Not reported. The network characteristics presented in Table 3 do not specify the number of pumps or valves for the four benchmark networks.
Network size classification: FOS: Small, semi-loop network. JILIN: Medium, semi-loop network. BWSN: Large, full-loop network. ZJ: Large, full-loop network.
Aim of study: The study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of Deep Q-Network (DQN) for determining optimal sensor locations in clean water distribution networks for contaminant detection. It further seeks to improve DQN performance through systematic hyperparameter optimisation using Grid Search and to assess the resulting sensor-placement strategies using detection coverage, detection time and cumulative reward. The study compares tuned DQN, untuned DQN and a Greedy Algorithm across multiple benchmark networks.
Simulation and experimental environment:
The experiments are conducted using simulated water distribution network datasets obtained from the University of Kentucky Water Distribution Systems database. Four benchmark networks—FOS (Fossiron), JILIN, ZJ and BWSN—are used to evaluate the proposed sensor-placement approach.

The network structures are represented as graphs consisting of nodes and links. Contamination scenarios are simulated using EPANET hydraulic modelling software, which models water flow and water-quality behaviour over time. Contaminant injection is represented as the release of a harmful substance at a specified network node over a defined time interval.

The DQN agent interacts with the simulated environment and selects sensor locations sequentially. Grid Search is subsequently applied to optimise selected DQN hyperparameters. The study compares the tuned DQN-based SPARC framework with an untuned DQN model and a Greedy Algorithm.

The authors report that the experiments were conducted in a controlled computational environment and provide hardware and software configurations in Table 4. The training configuration includes 1,000 episodes, a maximum of 10 placement steps per episode, a batch size of 32, a replay memory capacity of 2,000 transitions, a learning rate of 0.001, a discount factor of 0.99 and an epsilon decay rate of 0.995.
Notes:
The study uses four benchmark WDN datasets: FOS, JILIN, ZJ and BWSN. Although the experiments cover all four networks, the detailed sensor-placement maps and principal visualisations focus on FOS. Overall comparative results across the four networks are reported in Table 7.

The sensor budget is fixed at 10 sensors for every network. Consequently, the results represent a controlled comparison under a common sensor budget rather than an investigation of the optimal sensor count for each network.

The authors explicitly clarify that SPARC does not introduce a new reinforcement learning or optimisation algorithm. Its contribution is the application of DQN to sequential sensor placement and the systematic evaluation of tuned and untuned DQN configurations using Grid Search.
Main methodological contributions:
The study presents SPARC, a DQN-based framework for sequential sensor placement in water distribution networks for contaminant detection. Sensor placement is formulated as a Markov Decision Process in which the agent selects unoccupied network nodes sequentially until the fixed sensor budget is reached.

The framework integrates systematic Grid Search hyperparameter optimisation to investigate the effects of learning rate, discount factor, batch size and epsilon decay on DQN performance. It evaluates the tuned DQN model against an untuned DQN model and a Greedy Algorithm.

The study also provides a comparative assessment across four benchmark networks using detection coverage, detection time and cumulative reward. The authors emphasise that the contribution is a domain-specific and reproducible evaluation of DQN behaviour rather than the development of a new reinforcement learning algorithm.
Overall study findings:
The results indicate that SPARC demonstrates competitive contamination-detection performance compared with the Greedy Algorithm and the untuned DQN model, although its relative performance varies across the four benchmark networks. For FOS, SPARC achieves 81.08% detection coverage and an average detection time of 1.07 seconds, compared with 70.27% and 5.23 seconds for the Greedy Algorithm, and 78.38% and 2.07 seconds for the untuned DQN model. Across the four networks, SPARC generally achieves improved detection coverage, but it does not consistently outperform both comparison methods on every metric. For example, the Greedy Algorithm achieves higher coverage than SPARC on JILIN, while SPARC records a longer average detection time than both comparators on BWSN.

The statistical analysis reports a significant improvement in detection coverage, with p = 0.031 in the abstract and Table 6. However, the discussion section reports a different coverage p-value of 0.0423. The difference in average detection time is reported as statistically insignificant (p = 0.576). These findings suggest that Grid Search-based hyperparameter tuning improves the tested DQN configuration, particularly in detection coverage, but do not establish universal superiority over other sensor-placement algorithms.
Research gaps and future directions:
The authors identify several areas for further investigation:
1. Extending the evaluation to representative Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimisation, lean graph and integer-programming baselines.
2. Investigating the effects of different sensor budgets across networks of varying sizes.
3. Applying Bayesian Optimisation and Neural Architecture Search to improve computational efficiency in hyperparameter optimisation.
4. Extending the framework towards Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning to improve scalability and coordination.
5. Incorporating real-time flow dynamics and demand uncertainty.
6. Improving the framework's ability to handle larger and more complex water distribution networks.
The authors also identify the need to consider stochastic demand, uncertainty-aware contamination simulations, sensor reliability, heterogeneous installation costs and explicit feasibility constraints.
Study limitations:
The authors acknowledge several simplifying assumptions that limit the realism of the proposed framework.

The hydraulic and water-quality model is treated as deterministic, with fixed demand patterns and network parameters. Demand variability and parameter uncertainty are not explicitly modelled. Sensors are assumed to be perfectly reliable, without malfunction, communication failure or calibration drift.

The study also assumes homogeneous installation and maintenance costs and permits sensor placement at all demand nodes without explicitly representing forbidden locations or cost heterogeneity.

A fixed budget of 10 sensors is used across networks of different sizes. The authors acknowledge that larger networks, such as BWSN and ZJ, would likely require higher sensor budgets in practical deployments. Therefore, the results should be interpreted as methodological comparisons under a fixed budget rather than deployment-ready recommendations.

The comparator selection is also limited: the authors acknowledge that GA, PSO, lean graph and integer-programming approaches were not included in the main experimental comparison.
Reproducibility and data availability: The study uses publicly accessible water distribution network datasets from the University of Kentucky Water Distribution Systems database: https://www.uky.edu/WDST/database.html. EPANET is used for hydraulic and water-quality simulation. The authors provide details of the DQN architecture, hyperparameter optimisation procedure, sensor budget and experimental configuration. The article's Data Availability statement indicates that no datasets were generated or analysed during the study. A dedicated repository containing the SPARC source code, trained models or complete experimental outputs is not identified in the article. Consequently, the benchmark network data are publicly accessible, but the availability of the complete implementation and processed experimental artefacts cannot be confirmed.
RL algorithm:
Deep Q-Network (DQN).

The DQN agent learns a sensor-placement policy through interaction with a simulated water distribution network environment. Grid Search is used to optimise selected DQN hyperparameters. The proposed SPARC framework is therefore a DQN-based sensor-placement approach with systematic hyperparameter tuning.
RL architecture:
The DQN uses a feedforward neural network to approximate the action-value function \(Q(s,a)\), which estimates the expected cumulative reward for taking an action in a given state.

The architecture comprises:
- An input layer representing the current sensor-placement state as a binary vector.
- Two to three fully connected hidden layers, each containing between 64 and 256 neurons.
- ReLU activation functions in the hidden layers.
- An output layer producing Q-values for the feasible sensor-placement actions.
The agent selects the next sensor location based on the estimated Q-values for the available unoccupied nodes. The architecture uses experience replay, with a replay memory capacity of 2,000 transitions, and batch-based network updates.
Sensor placement approach:
Sensor placement is formulated as a sequential decision-making problem using a Markov Decision Process. The agent begins with an empty sensor configuration and selects one unoccupied network node at each decision step.

Each selected node is added to the current sensor configuration. The process continues until the fixed sensor budget of 10 sensors has been reached. The final configuration is therefore a set of 10 selected sensor locations.

The DQN learns which node to select based on the current sensor configuration and the reward received after each placement. Grid Search is subsequently used to identify a more effective hyperparameter configuration for the DQN agent.
State representation:
The state at time step \(t\) is represented by an N-dimensional binary vector:
\[
s_t=[x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_N]
\]
where \(N\) is the total number of nodes in the water distribution network.

Each element is defined as:
\[
x_i =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if a sensor has been placed at node } i\\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
The state therefore represents the current sensor-placement configuration and indicates which network nodes have already been selected.

The authors also classify the state as an intermediate state when fewer than \(K\) sensors have been placed and a terminal state when the required number of sensors has been reached.
Action space:
At each decision step, the agent selects one unoccupied network node as the next sensor location.

The available action set is:
\[
A(s_t)=\{i\in V\mid x_i=0\}
\]
where \(V\) represents the set of all network nodes.

If \(k\) sensors have already been placed, the number of available actions is:
\[
|A(s_t)|=N-k
\]
Each action adds one sensor to the current configuration. The process continues until the fixed budget of \(K=10\) sensors has been selected. Previously occupied nodes cannot be selected again.
Reward function:
The reward function encourages sensor placements that improve detection coverage and reduce average contamination detection time.

After placing a sensor at time step \(t\), the environment recalculates detection coverage \(C_t\) and average detection time \(T_t\). The changes are defined as:
\[
\Delta C_t=C_t-C_{t-1}
\]
\[
\Delta T_t=T_t-T_{t-1}
\]
The reward is:
\[
r_t=\alpha\cdot\Delta C_t-\beta\cdot\Delta T_t
\]
where:
- \(\alpha\) is the user-defined weight assigned to detection-coverage improvement.
- \(\beta\) is the user-defined weight assigned to detection-time reduction.
Positive rewards indicate improvements in overall detection performance, zero rewards indicate no net change, and negative rewards indicate degradation.

The authors explain that the DQN receives the continuous reward during training rather than converting it into a discrete positive, zero or negative reward.
Optimisation objectives:
The study formulates sensor placement as a multi-objective optimisation problem with two principal objectives:
1. Maximise detection coverage across contamination scenarios.
2. Minimise average contamination detection time.
The optimisation problem is expressed as:
\[
\max_{S\subseteq V} DC(S)
\]
\[
\min_{S\subseteq V} DT(S)
\]
subject to constraints including the available sensor budget and network topology.

Cumulative reward is also used to assess the learning performance of the DQN agent.
Comparator algorithms:
The proposed SPARC framework is compared against:
1. Greedy Algorithm: Selects sensor locations incrementally according to local coverage improvement.
2. Untuned DQN: A DQN model trained using its initial hyperparameter configuration without the Grid Search optimisation applied in SPARC.
The article does not include a direct experimental comparison against GA, PSO or integer programming. The authors explicitly acknowledge this as a limitation of the comparator selection.
Hyperparameter optimisation: The study employs Grid Search to systematically explore predefined DQN hyperparameter configurations. The parameters considered include learning rate (α), discount factor (γ), epsilon decay factor (ε), batch size and replay memory size. Each candidate configuration is trained and evaluated using detection coverage, average detection time and cumulative reward. The optimisation objective combines these performance measures, as expressed in Equation 19, to identify the best-performing configuration for the final experiments. The reported DQN training configuration includes a learning rate of 0.001, discount factor of 0.99, epsilon decay rate of 0.995, batch size of 32 and replay memory capacity of 2,000 transitions. However, the complete numerical search ranges and an unambiguous final optimal hyperparameter configuration are not reported.
RL training strategy:
The DQN agent is trained through repeated interaction with the simulated water distribution network environment. The initial training configuration comprises 1,000 episodes, with a maximum of 10 placement steps per episode, corresponding to the fixed sensor budget of \(K=10\). At each step, the agent selects an unoccupied network node using an epsilon-greedy policy, observes the resulting reward and next state, and stores the transition in an experience replay buffer.

The replay buffer has a capacity of 2,000 transitions, and batches of 32 samples are used to update the online Q-network. The initial learning rate is 0.001, the discount factor is 0.99, and the epsilon decay rate is 0.995. A separate target network is periodically synchronised with the online network to calculate target Q-values and support temporal-difference learning.

Grid Search evaluates predefined combinations of DQN hyperparameters. For each configuration, the DQN is trained and evaluated using detection coverage, average detection time and cumulative reward. The best-performing configuration is subsequently selected for the final sensor-placement evaluation.

The study reports 1,000 episodes for its initial DQN configuration. Figures 3 and 4 also display reward-convergence comparisons involving 1,000- and 2,000-episode training configurations. These should not be confused with the number of independent experimental runs.

The article describes gradient-descent parameter updates and also mentions the Adam optimiser. Do not assume that every experiment used one particular optimiser without further clarification.
Constraints on sensor placement:
The study imposes a fixed sensor-budget constraint:
\[
K=10
\]
Each episode involves selecting exactly 10 sensor locations. The agent selects only unoccupied nodes, preventing duplicate sensor placement at the same location.

The authors assume that sensors can be placed at all demand nodes. The framework does not explicitly encode forbidden locations, heterogeneous installation costs or location-specific feasibility constraints.

The authors also assume homogeneous installation and maintenance costs and perfectly reliable sensors.
Detection coverage:
Detection coverage
Detection coverage is defined as the percentage of contamination scenarios successfully detected:
\[
DC=\frac{N_d}{N_t}\times100\%
\]
where:
- \(N_d\) is the number of detected contamination scenarios.
- \(N_t\) is the total number of simulated contamination scenarios.

- Greedy Algorithm: 70.27%.
- Untuned DQN: 78.38%.
- SPARC: 81.08%.
The study also reports coverage results across JILIN, ZJ and BWSN in Table 7.

Sensor type and sensing modality: Water-quality sensors for detecting contaminant events in water distribution networks. The proposed placement approach selects network links (pipes) on which sensors are installed to detect contaminant propagation.
Study location: Not applicable (benchmark networks). The geographical locations of the four benchmark networks are not specified in the article.

The algorithm also defines a maximum sensor parameter \(K\), but the article does not provide a separate numerical value for \(K\) in the algorithm description. The ten selected locations in Table III establish the reported final sensor count.

FOS: 1 reservoir; tank count not reported.
ZJ: 1 reservoir; tank count not reported.
